text: Double/debiased machine learning removes the bias from regularization and overfitting in the nuisance estimates by combining Neyman-orthogonal scores with cross-fitting.

Chernozhukov et al. (2018, Table 2, Panel B) report partially linear DML estimates of the effect of 401(k) eligibility on net financial assets between $7,717 (lasso, 2-fold) and $9,247 (random forest, 5-fold) across seven nuisance learners.

With 5-fold cross-fitting and random forests, the published partially linear estimate is $9,247 with a split-adjusted standard error of 1,328 (median standard error 1,295) (Chernozhukov et al. 2018, Table 2, Panel B).
Without controls, the estimated difference in net financial assets by 401(k) eligibility is $19,559 with a standard error of 1,413.

The published estimates use the DML2 estimator with 2-fold and 5-fold cross-fitting, repeated over 100 random sample splits, and aggregate point estimates and standard errors across splits with the median method.

The outcome is net financial assets, the treatment is eligibility to enroll in a 401(k) plan, and the controls are age, income, family size, years of education, and indicators for marriage, two-earner household, defined-benefit pension, IRA participation and home ownership.
Chernozhukov et al. (2018) use the same 1991 SIPP data as Chernozhukov and Hansen (2004).
The authors' public replication repository distributes the data as sipp1991.dta, and its 401(k) script states that the sample selection and variable construction follow Abadie (2003).

As summarized by Chernozhukov et al. (2018), Poterba, Venti and Wise argue that 401(k) eligibility can be treated as exogenous after conditioning on income and other job-related observables, because around the time 401(k) plans became available workers were unlikely to choose employers on that basis.
Poterba, Venti and Wise (1995), using the 1984, 1987 and 1991 SIPP, find little evidence that 401(k) contributions substitute for other personal saving.

Chernozhukov and Hansen (2004) use 401(k) eligibility as an instrument for participation and find positive, significant quantile effects of participation on net financial assets across the distribution.
DoubleML implements the DML framework of Chernozhukov et al. (2018) as open-source software in Python and R.

The 401(k) partially linear model has been re-estimated with DML in software papers and documentation: ddml in Stata reports $9,748.79 (SE 1,331.36) with short-stacking, 4 folds and one resample; the DoubleML Python example reports $8,909.63 (SE 1,321.82) with random forests and 3 folds; Chernozhukov et al. (2026) report $9,002 (SE 1,394) with random forests.
An earlier run of the same exercise by the same authors gave a median 5-fold random-forest partially linear estimate of $9,252 (SE 1,400), within $5 of the 2018 published value.

Among the published and online re-analyses of the 401(k) data that we read, none reproduces Table 2, Panel B of Chernozhukov et al. (2018) cell by cell under its protocol (2- and 5-fold cross-fitting, 100 splits, median aggregation) with a side-by-side comparison; they use other fold counts, a single split, other estimators or other outcomes, or use the data only to calibrate simulations.

When rlasso is called with post = FALSE and a penalty list supplying c = 1.1 (as in the authors' code), hdm 0.1.0 and 0.2.0 reset the penalty constant to 0.5, hdm 0.2.3 keeps 1.1, and hdm 0.3.1 and 0.3.2 reset it to 0.5; rlassologit keeps the supplied c = 1.1 in all five CRAN versions.
The Table 2 estimates published in 2018 first appear in arXiv:1608.00060v5 (21 June 2017); version 4 (30 December 2016) reports an earlier run.
